evidence: src/infrastructure/http/createApp.ts: createApp({ orders, stock }: Controllers) maps routes only to controller methods (stock.list, orders.place, orders.pay, ...) and registers notFoundHandler/errorHandler.
src/infrastructure/http/requestParsing.ts: parseStateQuery calls the domain's isOrderStatus(value) and does not keep its own list of valid order states, so that rule stays in one place.

src/infrastructure/http/requestParsing.ts: the doc comment on parsePlaceOrderBody says 'Checks the shape of an untrusted request body; business rules are enforced by the domain', and the function checks only types (customerId string, lines array, productId string, quantity number).
Both parsers throw the shared ValidationError from domain/errors, which errorHandler is expected to turn into a response, so error handling is consistent across the module.
Graph: OrderController.ts imports requestParsing.ts and createApp.ts imports OrderController.ts, so both files are part of the same HTTP adapter.
parsedVerdict.reasoning: This module passes. Both files deal with one concern: the HTTP transport adapter. createApp.ts builds the Express app. It registers the health check, the stock routes and the order routes, using the Controllers abstraction, then adds the not-found and error middleware. requestParsing.ts turns untrusted request input into application commands and domain values, and the order controller in the same module imports it. Neither file repeats a rule that belongs somewhere else. parseStateQuery calls the domain's isOrderStatus instead of keeping its own list of valid states. parsePlaceOrderBody checks only the shape of the body and says in its doc comment that business rules are left to the domain. Both files report errors with the shared ValidationError, and createApp goes through the controller and middleware abstractions rather than handling requests inline. The only exception is the small /health endpoint, which is fine for app setup.
